cells.E: Recognition and route
cells.F: Input
cells.G: Output（example, not the truth)

cells.C: The manager wants an order-status lookup, but the order has not been uniquely identified.The manager should never need to remember an order ID before asking a quick question. The Co-pilot narrows the request with the smallest possible clarification and never guesses among similar orders.
cells.D:
User provides an incomplete order description
 → Search for matching orders
 → More than one record is found
 → Do not automatically select the first record
 → Present distinguishing information
 → Ask the user to clarify
 → Identify the selected order
 → Save it as the active order
cells.E:
Signals: customer name plus the singular phrase “the order”; no order ID or unique attribute. 
 Decision: identify a status-lookup request, search candidate orders, then ask for one distinguishing detail.
cells.F: Turn 1: Show me the TrendCart order./How is the TrendCart order doing?
cells.G: TrendCart has several active orders. Which one do you mean? You can identify it by order number, product, quantity, or due date.

cells.E:
Signals: product category supplied, but it may still match multiple rows.
 Decision: filter by customer and product; if multiple candidates remain, ask for the shortest useful discriminator.
cells.F: Turn 2: The scarf order.
cells.G: I found more than one TrendCart scarf order. Do you mean the [500-piece order due on 20 April] or the [800-piece order due later this month]?

cells.E:
Slots complete: customer, product, quantity, and due date identify one order.
 Decision: resolve the entity, set active_order, and retrieve its latest record before responding.
cells.F: Turn 3: The 500-piece order due on 20 April.
cells.G: That is [ORD-005]. Fresh record: [500 scarves], current stage [KNITTING], due [20 April 2026], latest recorded activity [24 March 2026].

cells.E:
Signals: contextual pronoun “it” plus a request for a delay judgement.
  Decision: resolve “it” to active_order; compare due date with current date; keep observed facts separate from a forecast.
cells.F: Turn 4: Is it already late?
cells.G: No. Its due date has not passed. However, it has had no recorded activity for [eight days], so I would flag it for attention rather than call it confirmed late.

cells.C: The manager assumes the Co-pilot remembers the order just discussed. The Co-pilot should preserve this context but refresh live fields before answering, so a convenient follow-up never returns stale information.
cells.D:
A prior order is active
→ Recognise a contextual follow-up
→ Keep the active order as the entity
→ Refresh the requested live field
→ State the current record and timestamp
→ Offer the next relevant check
cells.E:
Signals: pronoun ‘it’ follows an already resolved order; request concerns a live stage.
Decision: bind the request to active_order and refresh the stage field before responding.
cells.F: Turn 1: Has it moved on yet?
cells.G: I am checking the latest record for [ORD-005]. Its current recorded stage is [KNITTING], last updated on [24 March 2026].

cells.E:
Signals: manager asks for recency after a live-field answer.
Decision: retrieve the most recent event rather than infer progress from the stage alone.
cells.F: Turn 2: What was the last activity?
cells.G: The latest recorded activity is [machine allocation confirmed] on [24 March 2026]. There is no newer recorded production event.

cells.E:
Signals: ‘today’ requires a time-bounded verification.
Decision: search for events dated today; do not transform ‘no update’ into ‘no work happened’.
cells.F: Turn 3: Has anyone updated it today?
cells.G: I cannot see a recorded update for [ORD-005] today. That means the record is unchanged; it does not prove that no work has happened.

cells.E:
Signals: request shifts from fact lookup to a management decision.
Decision: state the observed condition, label the risk judgement, then offer a safe action.
cells.F: Turn 4: Should I chase it?
cells.G: I would flag it for follow-up because the record is unchanged and the due date is approaching. I can draft a chase-up message for your review if you want.

cells.B: 1.3 Assess order risk and trace it
cells.C: A risk label must be explainable and must not be confused with a confirmed failure.
cells.D: Refresh order → compare due date and activity → state risk → trace back to source fields.
cells.E: ‘It’ refers to an active order and asks for a judgement. Refresh before assessing.
cells.F: Turn 1: Is it at risk?
cells.G: It needs attention because it has no recorded activity for [eight days]. Its due date has not passed, so this is a risk flag, not confirmed lateness.

cells.E: Manager asks why the risk exists. Trace specific fields and dates.
cells.F: Turn 2 : Why did you flag it?
cells.G: The flag uses [latest activity date], [days since activity], and [due date].

cells.E: Manager asks whether outcome is certain. Separate observed fact from forecast.
cells.F: Turn 3 : So it will be late?
cells.G: Not necessarily. The record shows a risk pattern, but it does not establish a confirmed late delivery.

cells.E: Manager requests provenance. Present activity history.
cells.F: Turn 4: Show the activity history.
cells.G: I will show the timestamped activity history for [ORD-005], with the latest event highlighted.

cells.C: When two orders compete for attention, the manager needs a transparent comparison rather than an opaque score.
cells.D: Load both orders → compare requested fields → resolve ambiguous pronouns → select one for action.
cells.E: Two order IDs are supplied. Ask which comparison dimension matters.
cells.F: Turn 1 : Compare ORD-005 and ORD-021.
cells.G: Which aspect matters most: due date, stage, latest activity, or recorded risk?

cells.E: Manager specifies fields. Return side-by-side facts with labels.
cells.F: Turn 2: Due date and recent updates.
cells.G: [ORD-005]: due [date], latest update [date]. [ORD-021]: due [date], latest update [date].

cells.E: ‘It’ is ambiguous after comparison. Ask, do not guess.
cells.F: Turn 3 : Which one is more risky?
cells.G: I can assess both. Should I prioritise by due-date pressure, recorded blockers, or update recency?

cells.E: Manager chooses criterion. Apply transparent rule and recommend.
cells.F: Turn 4 : Prioritise the nearest deadline.
cells.G: On that criterion, [selected order] should be reviewed first because it is due [sooner].

cells.C: The manager needs a conditional capacity estimate before promising a customer.
cells.D: Clarify delivery requirement → retrieve load and rates → estimate feasibility → state assumptions → test contingency → recommend.
cells.E: New-order feasibility request; delivery point is a material missing constraint.
cells.F: Turn 1 : Can we take 800 hoodies by the 25th?
cells.G: Does ‘by the 25th’ mean ready at our factory or delivered to the customer?

cells.E: Delivery point clarified. Call capacity and throughput tools; do not calculate in narration.
cells.F: Turn 2 : Delivered to the customer.
cells.G: Preliminary estimate: [feasible / not feasible / feasible with conditions]. The limiting stage is [stage].

cells.E: Manager asks for assumptions. Expose data-derived and controllable inputs.
cells.F: Turn 3 : What assumptions did you use?
cells.G: I used [working days], comparable recent stage rates, current load, and [delivery buffer].

cells.E: Manager tests a disruption. Rerun under named scenario.
cells.F: Turn 4: What if packing loses one day?
cells.G: Under that scenario, the result becomes [result]; the main effect is [delay / reduced buffer].

cells.E: Manager seeks customer-facing decision. Give bounded recommendation.
cells.F: Turn 5 : What should I tell the customer?
cells.G: Recommend [accept only if condition X / offer later date / decline]. I can draft the response with the condition stated clearly.

cells.B: 1.6 Prioritise a daily exception list（感觉和晨报的功能有重合？）
cells.C: The manager wants a fast start-of-day view, not a raw dump of every order. The Co-pilot should clarify the operating window, apply a transparent priority rule, and surface why each item needs attention.
cells.D:
Manager asks what needs attention
→ Recognise a prioritisation intent
→ Clarify time window and scope if absent
→ Retrieve candidate exceptions
→ Rank by an explainable rule
→ Show evidence for each priority
→ Let the manager drill into one order
cells.E:
Signals: broad phrase ‘needs attention’ with no time boundary.
Decision: classify as prioritisation, ask for a concise time window, and avoid choosing an arbitrary list.
cells.F: Turn 1: What needs attention today?
cells.G: Do you want items due today only, or the next [seven days] as well? I can prioritise by due-date pressure, missing updates, and recorded blockers.

cells.E:
Signals: a time window is supplied.
Decision: retrieve orders in scope and compute an explainable priority ordering from recorded facts.
cells.F: Turn 2: Include the next seven days.
cells.G: I found [three] orders to review first: [ORD-014] due tomorrow with no update for [six days]; [ORD-005] due in [ten days] with no update for [eight days]; and [ORD-021] with a recorded material blocker.

cells.E:
Signals: the manager challenges the rank of one item.
Decision: reveal the evidence used in the ordering; do not hide the rule behind an opaque score.
cells.F: Turn 3: Why is ORD-014 first?
cells.G: [ORD-014] is first because its due date is closest and its latest recorded activity is older than the review threshold. The ranking reflects urgency, not a prediction that it will fail.

cells.E:
Signals: the manager selects an item from the list.
Decision: set the selected item as active_order and move into the requested detail view.
cells.F: Turn 4: Open ORD-014.
cells.G: [ORD-014] is now the active order. Its latest record shows [current stage], [due date], and [last recorded activity]. What would you like to check next?

cells.B: 2.1 Check whether a stage output is normal
cells.C: A production number is useful only when compared against a valid baseline.
cells.D: Identify stage and date → define a fair comparison → run normality tool → state result and limits.
cells.E: Normal’ is a judgement request, but the comparison baseline is missing.
cells.F: Turn 1 : Is packing output of 800 pieces normal?
cells.G: Do you mean today’s output? I can compare it with the same weekday in recent working weeks.

cells.E: Manager accepts the comparison. Use the judgement tool, not a simple average across non-working days.
cells.F: Turn 2: Yes, use the same weekday.
cells.G: [800 pieces] is [within / below / above] the comparison range for the selected same-weekday records.

cells.E: Manager asks for meaning. Translate the result into a proportionate management check.
cells.F: Turn 3: Should I worry about it?
cells.G: Review it today if the lower output repeats or threatens near-due orders. One low observation alone is a signal to check, not proof of a sustained problem.

cells.E: Manager asks for evidence. Surface the rows behind the comparison.
cells.F: Turn 4: Show me the records behind it.
cells.G: I will show the selected production-log rows with [date], [stage], and [output].

cells.C: The manager needs an evidence-led explanation, not an invented cause.
cells.D: Retrieve related records → show co-occurring facts → distinguish pattern from cause → propose a check.
cells.E: ‘Why’ may request causality. Retrieve related facts before explaining.
cells.F: Turn 1: Why was packing output lower yesterday?
cells.G: I will check the packing log and related upstream records for that day.

cells.E: Records are available. Present observed co-occurrences, not a causal claim.
cells.F: Turn 2: What did you find?
cells.G: The records show [lower upstream output] and [a recorded blocker] on the same day. These may help explain the pattern, but the log does not prove a single cause.

cells.E: Manager requests raw evidence. Show source rows distinctly from interpretation.
cells.F: Turn 3 : Show the raw records.
cells.G: Here are the relevant rows: [date / stage / output / recorded event].

cells.E: Manager needs a next step. Recommend an evidence-proportionate operational check.
cells.F: Turn 4 : What should we check next?
cells.G: First verify whether the [blocker] is still active and whether upstream output has recovered today.

cells.B: 3.1 Draft, revise, and send a chase-up
cells.C: Drafting should be easy; sending must be explicitly confirmed and logged.
cells.D: Verify order → draft only → revise → preview recipient and final text → confirm → send and log.
cells.E: Manager asks to chase. Verify factual trigger before drafting.
cells.F: Turn 1: ORD-005 has not moved for a week. What should we do?
cells.G: The record shows no activity for [one week]. I recommend requesting a status and recovery plan; I can draft it.

cells.E: ]Drafting authorised, not sending. Capture recipient and tone.
cells.F: Turn 2: Draft it to Maya, firm but polite.
cells.G: Draft to Maya: ‘Please provide an updated status, recovery plan, and expected completion date for [ORD-005].’

cells.E: Targeted revision requested. Update unsent draft.
cells.F: Turn 3: Ask for an answer by tomorrow noon.
cells.G: Revised draft includes: ‘Please respond by [tomorrow, 12:00 p.m.].’ It remains unsent.

cells.E: External send requested. Require explicit confirmation.
cells.F: Turn 4 : Send it.
cells.G: Ready to send the revised message to [Maya] about [ORD-005]. Please confirm ‘send now’.

cells.E: Explicit confirmation. Send, then record actual result.
cells.F: Turn 5 : Send now.
cells.G: Message sent. Recipient, final text, and send time were recorded in the order history.

cells.C: Internal notes must be attached to the right order and never confused with an external message.
cells.D: Identify target order → capture note → classify as internal → preview → confirm → save with timestamp.
cells.E: Manager requests a note but target needs confirmation.
cells.F: Turn 1: Add a note that we escalated this today.
cells.G: I can add an internal note to [active order: ORD-005]. Is that the correct order?

cells.E: Target confirmed. Present exact internal note before saving.
cells.F: Turn 2: Yes, ORD-005.
cells.G: Proposed internal note: ‘Escalated with supplier on [date]; awaiting status and recovery plan.’ Please confirm to save.

cells.E: Explicit confirmation. Save as internal only and log timestamp.
cells.F: Turn 3: Save it.
cells.G: Internal note saved to [ORD-005] with today’s timestamp. It was not sent externally.

cells.C: The manager should not need to remember to re-check a risk. A reminder should monitor a defined condition and alert only when needed.
cells.D: Capture order and condition → resolve relative date → preview trigger → confirm → create and log reminder.
cells.E: Conditional monitoring request with relative deadline. Resolve date and ask for missing time if needed.
cells.F: Turn 1 : If there is no reply by tomorrow noon, remind me.
cells.G: I will check whether [ORD-005] has a recorded reply by [tomorrow, 12:00 p.m., explicit date]. Please confirm to create this reminder.

cells.E: Manager changes scheduling detail. Update the proposed reminder; do not create one yet.
cells.F: Turn 2: Make it 2 p.m. instead.
cells.G: Updated reminder: check [ORD-005] at [2:00 p.m. on explicit date] and notify you only if no reply is recorded.

cells.E: Explicit confirmation. Create condition, schedule, and order link.
cells.F: Turn 3 : Confirm.
cells.G: Reminder created for [ORD-005]. It will notify you only if the reply condition remains unmet.

cells.E: Manager requests later change. Locate existing reminder and update it rather than duplicating it.
cells.F: Turn 4 : Move it to Friday morning.
cells.G: I found the existing reminder for [ORD-005]. What time on Friday morning would you prefer?
